title: Embeddings and similarity
subtitle: Turning meaning into distance
mission: Find out who lives near whom on the model’s map of meanings. Then find a word that doesn’t know where to live.

predict.question: guess: on the map of meanings, “cat” is closer to…

feedback.right: yes! “Cat” lives right next to “dog”, far from “car”. The map is organized by meaning, not spelling.
feedback.wrong: close! Look at the map: “cat” sits right next to “dog” and far from “car”. Similar letters don’t matter; meaning does.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Look at the map: “cat” lives next to “dog”, far from “car”. It’s meaning, not spelling.

coach.ui: guess noted. Keep “cat” and hit Run.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run the command below.

tryNext.ui: Now try “banana” and “car”, and raise “Neighbors” to 5.
tryNext.cmd: Now try near "banana" --top 5 and then near "car".

why.simples:
Imagine every word is a little house on a map. Words about similar things live in the same neighborhood: animals on one side, fruits on the other.
To know if two words go together, the computer just measures the distance between the houses.
why.dev:
An embedding model turns text into a vector of numbers (hundreds or thousands of dimensions). Texts with similar meaning become nearby vectors.
Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity. Here there are only 2 dimensions and hand-made coordinates, to fit the screen; the similarity shown is 1 − normalized distance.
why.especialista:
Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations, deduplication and RAG (step 6). Pick the model by domain and language, and normalize vectors if you’ll use dot product.
One vector per text blends meanings: ambiguous words and long texts become an average. That’s why documents are split into chunks and vector search is combined with keyword search (hybrid search).

mission.ui: time to break it. Tap “bat” and run.
mission.cmd: time to break it. Run near "bat" --top 4.

break.success: Broken: is “{word}” an animal or a baseball bat? With a single point it sits halfway, and its neighbors come from two neighborhoods. Real models do better by looking at the whole sentence, not just the word.
break.calm: “{word}” has one meaning, so its neighbors share a neighborhood. Look for a word with two meanings.

ui: Pick a word from the examples and hit Run.
“Neighbors” sets how many nearest words appear.
cmd: The word goes in quotes, after near.
--top sets how many neighbors to show.

errors.aboveMax.top: Up to 8 neighbors, or the map turns into a spider web.
errors.belowMin.top: At least 1 neighbor, or there’s nothing to compare with.
errors.model.unknownWord: “{value}” isn’t on my little word map. Real models have a vector for any text; this toy only knows the words on the map.

scene.label: The map of meanings
scene.mapAria: Two-dimensional word map; words with similar meanings sit close together

steps: Ask an AI chat: list 5 words similar in meaning to “cat” and 5 to “bat”.
Notice whether it separates the two meanings of “bat” (or asks which one you mean).
In the Practice track you’ll compute real embeddings in the browser.
recipe.ok: for “cat” you get only animals; for “bat” you get animals and sports gear (or a question about the meaning).
